title: Core Policy Coupled to Concrete Infrastructure Adapters
pattern: Stable business or domain policy directly imports, instantiates, or calls volatile concrete databases, frameworks, serializers, logging implementations, or device adapters rather than depending on policy-appropriate interfaces.
why_bad: Changes in infrastructure contracts (e.g., a database client upgrade, a table restructuring, or replacing the storage engine) can propagate into core policy, coupling high-value logic to low-level machinery and widening the scope of changes and rebuilding.
detection: Inspect core-domain modules for imports (`use`, `import`) and actual usage of concrete infrastructure clients such as database drivers (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis), HTTP frameworks, serialization libraries, or cloud SDKs. Confirm that business policy depends on the concrete detail; a directory name or an import in an adapter is not by itself a violation.
counterexample: Infrastructure adapters and composition/entry points that intentionally construct and wire concrete dependencies; stable language primitives, standard error formats, or ubiquitous runtime facilities (like `std::time`) that do not bind policy to a particular external device or storage implementation.
source: Robert C. Martin, *Clean Architecture* (2017), Chapter 11 ("Dependency Inversion Principle"), pp. 87-88; Robert C. Martin, *Clean Architecture* (2017), Chapter 14, "Component Coupling: The Dependency Inversion Principle", p. 263, 265.
